idiom_name: scala.concurrent.Future + ExecutionContext (Promise for the write side)
implementation_notes: scala.concurrent ships the pattern: Future { work }(ec) starts the computation on the ExecutionContext's pool and returns Future[T] immediately; the value is collected by composition (map/flatMap/zip, for-comprehensions) or, when blocking is genuinely required, by Await.result(f, duration), which rethrows the failure. A Future is completed exactly once and never overwritten, so it is the pattern's AsyncResult handle; Promise[T] is the write side used when completion is driven by a callback (wrapping a Java listener, for instance) - the caller hands the promise's future to the consumer and completes the promise when the callback fires. There is no async/await in the standard language, so continuations are expressed with combinators and onComplete callbacks (the latter are the discouraged, callback-style form). Effect systems such as Cats Effect and ZIO are the modern alternative, adding cancellation and resource safety that bare Future lacks.
pitfalls: ExecutionContext.global is a fork-join pool sized for CPU work: blocking calls inside a future starve it (and can deadlock it) unless wrapped in blocking { } or moved to a dedicated execution context.
A failed Future that nobody composes is silently discarded; onComplete/onFailure or a strict combinator is required to observe the failure.
Await.result from inside the same pool that must run the awaited future deadlocks; blocking collection belongs outside the pool, or nowhere.
Futures start eagerly at creation and cannot be cancelled once running without an effect system, so a dropped handle still consumes resources.
An implicit ExecutionContext makes thread placement invisible: inject a deterministic one in tests, otherwise timing assumptions leak into behaviour.
